document_sections.heading: 1.1 Aim and scope
document_sections.content: These updated European Association of Urology (EAU) Guidelines address management of upper urinary tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC). Separate EAU guidance covers non-muscleinvasive bladder cancer, muscle-invasive and metastatic bladder cancer (MIBC), and primary urethral carcinoma. Recommendations present the evidence available to the panel but do not guarantee the best outcome for an individual. Clinical judgment, patient values and individual circumstances remain essential; the guidelines are neither mandatory instructions nor a legal standard of care.

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Panel composition
document_sections.content: The document describes an international multidisciplinary panel comprising clinicians from relevant specialties and a patient representative. The panel was selected for expertise in caring for people suspected of having urothelial carcinoma (UC).

document_sections.heading: 1.3 Available publications
document_sections.content: An abbreviated Pocket Guidelines version is available, but its use may require consultation of the full guidelines. The document also points to scientific publications, including a scientific summary published in 2021.

document_sections.heading: 1.4 Publication history & summary of changes
document_sections.content: The first EAU Guidelines on UTUC appeared in 2011. Newly published literature is assessed annually to inform revisions. The 2024 guidance updates the 2023 version.

document_sections.heading: 1.4.1 Summary of changes
document_sections.content: For 2024, the panel identified, assembled and assessed new evidence across the guidelines. Changes concern genetic risk and the implications of Lynch syndrome-related UTUC, the molecular characteristics of UTUC, tumour location and the roles of multifocality, size and hydronephrosis, clinical risk stratification, and management of distant metastases.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Data identification
document_sections.content: For the 2023 guidelines, a structured literature assessment searched Pubmed, Ovid, EMBASE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews for articles published between May 4th 2022 and May 1st 2023. After duplicate removal, 333 distinct records were obtained and screened. Basic research, case series, reports and editorial comments were excluded. Most identified publications were retrospective, although some were large multicentre studies. Because randomised evidence was scarce, selection considered changes in clinical concepts, intermediateand long-term outcomes, study quality and relevance; older work was included only for historical importance. Recommendation strength reflects the balance of benefits and harms, evidence quality and estimate certainty, and patient values and preferences. Assessment also considers effect size, precision, consistency, heterogeneity and other study-related factors. Strong usually denotes higher-quality evidence and/or a favourable benefit–harm balance consistent with patient preferences; Weak usually reflects less certain evidence or benefit–harm balance and/or variability in preferences.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Review
document_sections.content: The UTUC guidelines underwent peer review before their 2023 publication.

document_sections.heading: 3.1 Epidemiology
document_sections.content: UC is the second most frequent urological malignancy in developed countries and can arise in the lower urinary tract or the pyelocaliceal cavities and ureter. Bladder cancer (BC) constitutes 90–95% of UC, whereas UTUC constitutes 5–10%; estimated annual incidence in Western countries is almost two cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Incidence has increased over recent decades, possibly because detection improved and populations aged. Incidence peaks at 70–90 years, and UTUC occurs twice as often in men. In an international retrospective registry of 2,380 people diagnosed between 2014 and 2019 at 101 centres in 29 countries, 70.5% were men, 53.3% were current or former smokers, and 53% received a diagnosis after symptoms, chiefly visible haematuria. A meta-analysis of 44 studies estimated UTUC incidence among people with visible and non-visible haematuria at 0.75% and 0.17%, respectively. Approximately two-thirds of patients presenting with UTUC have muscle-invasive disease at diagnosis, versus 15–25% with newly diagnosed BC; population studies from Germany and England suggest muscle-invasive UTUC accounts for approximately half of recent incident cases. Approximately 9% present with metastases. Pyelocaliceal tumours occur approximately twice as frequently as ureteral tumours; multifocality occurs in approximately 10–20%, and concomitant upper-tract carcinoma in situ in between 11% and 36%. Concurrent BC occurs in 17%; previous BC was recorded in 41% of American men and 4% of Chinese men. These differences, alongside genetic and epigenetic factors, may help explain more advanced, higher-grade presentations in Asian patients. After treatment, bladder recurrence occurs in 29%, varying with patient, tumour and treatment characteristics, versus 2–5% recurrence in the contralateral upper tract. UTUC and BC differ substantially in frequencies of common genomic changes, although tumours in a person with both cancers are often clonally related. UTUC genomic profiling can inform bladder-recurrence risk and identify Lynch syndrome-associated tumours. Among 82 patients given intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) for high-risk BC and imaged regularly between years 1 and 3, 13% developed asymptomatic UTUC; another series of 307 patients without routine upper-tract imaging reported 25% UTUC after BC. A multicentre cohort of n = 402 followed for 50 month reported 7.5% UTUC among NMIBC recipients of BCG; intravesical recurrence and a non-papillary tumour at transurethral resection of the bladder (TURB) predicted UTUC. Following radical cystectomy for MIBC, 3–5% develop metachronous UTUC.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.1 Environmental risk factors
document_sections.content: Evidence establishing causation for proposed environmental risks is generally weak except for tobacco and aristolochic acid. Tobacco exposure increases relative UTUC risk 2.5 to 7.0 fold. A population study including 229,251 relatives of UC cases and 1,197,552 relatives of matched controls found familial aggregation independent of smoking-related behaviour, but not for UTUC, which represented more than 9% of its cohort; the authors inferred that familial aggregation of UC may concern the lower tract specifically. Aristolochic acid from aristolochia plants can irreversibly injure renal proximal tubules, producing chronic tubulointerstitial disease, and its mutagenicity can lead to UTUC. Exposure can occur through agricultural contamination, as described for Balkan endemic nephropathy, or through aristolochiabased herbal remedies. Following bioactivation, persistent aristolactam-deoxyadenosine DNA adducts provide exposure markers and produce a characteristic spectrum dominated by A>T transversions on the non-transcribed DNA strand. Aristolochic acid has also been linked with BC, renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Less than 10% of exposed people are estimated to develop UTUC. Two retrospective series found aristolochic acid-associated UTUC more frequent in females, whose prognosis nevertheless exceeded that of affected males. Arsenic in drinking water together with aristolochia-based remedies appears to produce an additive carcinogenic effect; links between drinking-water arsenic and UTUC in Taiwan and Chile remain tentative. Alcohol may also be associated with UTUC: a case-control study of 1,569 cases and 506,797 controls found significantly greater risk among ever-drinkers than never-drinkers (OR: 1.23; 95% CI: 1.08–1.40, p = 0.001), identified a risk threshold of > 15 g of alcohol/day relative to never-drinkers, and observed a dose–response relationship.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.2 Genetic risk factors
document_sections.content: Lynch syndrome predisposes to early colorectal and several extra-colonic cancers through pathogenic germline changes in one allele of MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2. UTUC is the 3rd most common Lynch-spectrum malignancy after colorectal and endometrial cancers. Recognition matters to carriers and relatives because of subsequent multiple-cancer risk and strong hereditary predisposition. Germline MMR mutations occur in 9% of UTUC patients versus 1% with BC; most associated tumours arise in MSH2 and MSH6 carriers. Somatic alteration of the other allele produces deficient MMR (dMMR), loss of the corresponding protein on immunochemistry, and potentially microsatellite instability detectable by PCR. PREMM5 estimates an individual's cumulative probability of carrying a Lynch-related germline mutation; Amsterdam II criteria remain the predominant means of identifying higher-risk families. Those criteria require at least three relatives with Lynch-associated cancer involving colorectum, endometrium, small bowel or UTUC; one must be a first-degree relative of the other two, at least two successive generations must be affected, at least one diagnosis must occur before age 50, familial adenomatous polyposis must be excluded in colorectal cases, and diagnoses must have pathological confirmation. Among 115 consecutive UTUC patients, 13.9% screened positive under Amsterdam II and 5.2% had confirmed Lynch syndrome. Another UTUC study suggested that age <60 at initial diagnosis and personal history of another Lynch-related malignancy could each indicate increased risk. A proposed simplified tool combines those criteria with one first-degree relative diagnosed with Lynch-related cancer before 50 or two first-degree relatives with Lynch-related cancer at any age; it could identify suspected Lynch-related disease in more than 20% of UTUC patients. Patients meeting clinical high-risk criteria should receive germline DNA sequencing and family counselling. Because clinical criteria have limited diagnostic performance, even patients without suspected genetic predisposition could undergo PCR testing for MSI or immunochemistry for dMMR; a positive result likewise calls for germline sequencing and family counselling. Figure 3.1 depicts interview-based selection, possible tumour MMR screening, germline testing and subsequent clinical evaluation, close monitoring and family counselling; it reports germ-line mutations in 5–9%. The figure's protein list uses PSM2, whereas the surrounding discussion uses PMS2. In Chinese patients, germline mutations in MSH2, BRCA2, BRCA1 and BRIP1 have been shown to significantly increase UTUC risk. Differences in carcinogen exposure and susceptibility, including smoking, may influence expression of genetic predisposition. Some polymorphisms are linked to greater cancer risk or faster progression; two UTUC-specific polymorphisms have been reported. UTUC may share some risk factors and molecular pathways with bladder UC.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.3 History of bladder cancer
document_sections.content: Prior BC is associated with increased UTUC risk. Patients requiring ureteral stenting during TURB, including before radical cystectomy, have shown greater upper-tract recurrence risk.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.1 Histological types
document_sections.content: Upper-tract tumours are nearly always UC; exclusively non-urothelial histology is unusual, although histological subtypes occur in approximately 25% of UTUC. Pure urinary-tract squamous cell carcinoma is often thought to relate to chronic inflammation or infection arising from urolithiasis. Divergent squamous differentiation within UC occurs in approximately 15%. Keratinising squamous metaplasia raises squamous-cancer risk and therefore requires surveillance. UTUC with histological subtypes is high-grade and has a poorer prognosis than pure UC. Other rare subtypes include sarcomatoid; inverted growth is also described as frequent in the upper urinary tract. Collecting duct carcinomas can resemble UC but have a distinctive renal-cancer-like transcriptomic signature and a proposed origin in distal convoluted tubules; they are classified as renal tumours.

document_sections.heading: 3.4 Molecular background of UTUCs
document_sections.content: Studies of DNA, RNA and protein expression identify genetically distinct UTUC groups. Frequently reported alterations involve FGFR3, chromatin-remodelling genes KMT2D and KDM6A, TP53/MDM2, and genes including CDKN2A or RAS. Activating FGFR3 mutations occur in > 90% tumours in the low-grade group, which has fewer TP53/MDM2 mutations; high-grade disease often has TP53-pathway alterations. UTUC has also been reported to have depleted T-cell immune contexture and activated FGFR3 signalling. Five molecular subtypes differ in expression, location and outcome, but whether treatment responses differ is unknown, limiting routine clinical usefulness.

document_sections.heading: 3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for epidemiology, aetiology, and histology
document_sections.content: The evidence summary assigns LE 2a to increased UTUC risk with aristolochic acid or smoking exposure and to UTUC risk in Lynch syndrome. The recommendations are to assess personal and family history using modified Amsterdam II criteria for Lynch syndrome screening (Strong), perform germline DNA sequencing if hereditary UTUC is clinically suspected (Weak), and offer MMR-protein or microsatellite-instability testing when hereditary UTUC is not clinically suspected (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 4.1 Classification
document_sections.content: UTUC and BC have similar classification and morphology. Limited biopsy samples often prevent reliable differentiation of non-invasive papillary disease, flat carcinoma in situ (CIS) and invasive carcinoma. Histological grade is consequently used in clinical decisions because of its strong association with pathological stage.

document_sections.heading: 4.2 Tumour Node Metastasis staging
document_sections.content: Table 1 presents TNM classification 2017. Regional lymph nodes comprise hilar and retroperitoneal nodes and, for mid- or distal-ureter tumours, pelvic nodes. N classification does not depend on laterality. The table defines primary-tumour, regional-node and distant-metastasis categories, including site-specific T3 definitions and lymph-node size criteria.

document_sections.heading: 4.3 Tumour grade
document_sections.content: WHO and the International Society of Urological Pathology introduced a UC histological classification in 2004 and 2016 that stratifies patients differently from the 1973 WHO system. A 2022 revision of the 2004/2016 WHO grading system made no major changes. These guidelines retain both the 1973 and 2004/2016 WHO classifications because most published evidence uses the 1973 system.

document_sections.heading: 5.1 Symptoms
document_sections.content: UTUC may be found incidentally or investigated because of symptoms. Obstruction by clot or tumour can cause flank pain in 20–32%. Anorexia, weight loss, malaise, fatigue, fever, night sweats or cough in someone with UTUC should trigger assessment for metastases, which carry a poorer prognosis. Symptoms at diagnosis are associated with worse prognosis.

document_sections.heading: 5.2.1 Computed tomography
document_sections.content: Computed tomography (CT) urography is the most diagnostically accurate available imaging modality. A meta-analysis covering 13 studies and 1,233 patients estimated pooled UTUC sensitivity at 92% (CI: 0.85–0.96) and specificity at 95% (CI: 0.88–0.98). Rapid thin-section acquisition permits multiplanar, high-resolution isotropic assessment. Flat epithelial lesions lacking mass effect or urothelial thickening generally cannot be seen on CT. Enlarged lymph nodes on CT strongly predict UTUC metastases.

document_sections.heading: 5.2.2 Magnetic resonance urography
document_sections.content: Magnetic resonance (MR) urography is indicated when CT urography cannot be performed, usually because radiation or iodinated contrast is contraindicated. With contrast, its sensitivity for tumours < 2 cm is 75%. CT urography has higher sensitivity and specificity than MR urography for UTUC diagnosis and staging.

document_sections.heading: 5.2.3 18F-Fluorodeoxglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography
document_sections.content: A retrospective multicentre investigation of 117 surgically treated UTUC patients reported 82% sensitivity and 84% specificity for detecting nodal metastases with 18F-Fluorodeoxglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT). Suspicious nodes were linked to worse recurrence-free survival. Validation and comparisons against MR and CT remain necessary. FDG-PET can also assess nodal and distant metastases when renal impairment or allergy makes iodinated contrast unsuitable.

document_sections.heading: 5.3 Cystoscopy
document_sections.content: Urethrocystoscopy forms part of UTUC investigation to exclude coexisting BC.

document_sections.heading: 5.4 Cytology and urinary markers
document_sections.content: Abnormal cytology with normal bladder cystoscopy and no bladder or prostatic-urethral CIS may indicate high-grade UTUC. Cytology from the affected upper tract is more sensitive than voided urine cytology. One study detected up to 91% of cancers by barbotage cytology. Samples from renal cavities and the ureter should preferably precede contrast administration for retrograde ureteropyelography because contrast can impair specimens; retrograde ureteropyelography remains a diagnostic option. FISH sensitivity for molecular abnormalities characteristic of UTUC is approximately 72–84%. A systematic review of 25 studies found cytology and FISH the most frequently investigated tests; FISH specificity was comparable to cytology at 80-100%, with sensitivity of 35-86% versus 11-71% for cytology. Review authors considered both tests inadequate to rule out cancer/UTUC because of broad performance ranges. In a prospective study of 79 patients with suspected UTUC using upper-tract urine obtained just before URS, sensitivities for Xpert Bladder, FISH, Bladder Epicheck and cytology were respectively 100%, 87%, 64% and 42%, and specificities were 4%, 82%, 79% and 94%. FISH, Bladder Epicheck and cytology may assist detection, but well-designed prospective comparative studies must confirm their utility.

document_sections.heading: 5.5 Diagnostic ureteroscopy
document_sections.content: Flexible ureteroscopy (URS) can visualise the ureter, renal pelvis and collecting system, obtain suspicious-lesion biopsies and, when needed, confirm UTUC. It is also essential for detailed tumour mapping before kidney preservation, assessing presence, appearance, number and size of lesions. Ureteroscopic biopsy identifies grade in more than 90% of cases with a low false-negative rate regardless of sample size, although grade can be underestimated relative to nephroureterectomy; second-look URS is therefore necessary in follow-up after kidney-sparing treatment. URS permits selective ureteral cytology. Biopsy staging can be inaccurate, so biopsy grade, imaging and cytology may jointly inform the choice between radical nephroureterectomy (RNU) and kidney-sparing therapy. In a meta-analysis comparing pre-RNU URS with no URS, 8 out of 12 studies reported more intravesical recurrences after URS; URS biopsy was also identified as a risk factor. Another review of 16 studies found no significant association for URS alone, but significantly increased intravesical recurrence after URS plus biopsy, without an effect on overall survival or non-urothelial recurrence. A study is needed to determine whether immediate intravesical chemotherapy after URS with biopsy or laser treatment reduces post-RNU bladder recurrence. Improved flexible instruments and newer imaging may aid detection of flat lesions. Narrow-band imaging is promising but preliminary; optical coherence tomography and confocal laser endomicroscopy (Cellvizio®) have shown promising correspondence with definitive histology for high-grade UTUC grading and/or staging.

document_sections.heading: 5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of UTUC
document_sections.content: The evidence summary identifies CT urography together with URS as the best approach to UTUC diagnosis and staging (LE 2a), high sensitivity of selective cytology for high-grade tumours including CIS (LE 3), and detection of concurrent BC by urethrocystoscopy (LE 2a). Recommended actions are urethrocystoscopy to exclude a bladder tumour (Strong); chest, abdominal and pelvic assessment with CT urography for diagnosis and staging (Strong); diagnostic URS if imaging and voided cytology cannot adequately establish diagnosis and/or risk category (Strong); and possible MR urography or 18F-Fluorodeoxglucose positron emission tomography/CT when CT is contraindicated (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.1 Prognostic factors
document_sections.content: Patient- and tumour-related prognostic features can guide selection between radical and kidney-sparing local treatment and inform discussion of peri-operative systemic therapy.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1.1 Age and gender
document_sections.content: Older age at RNU independently predicts poorer cancer-specific survival (CSS). Gender has not been shown to affect UTUC prognosis.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1.2 Ethnicity
document_sections.content: An international academic-centre study found no racial outcome differences. In contrast, U.S. population studies indicated poorer outcomes in African-American patients than in other ethnic groups; whether access to care or biology explains this remains unclear. Another study identified differences between Chinese and American patients in presenting risks, disease features and predictors of unfavourable oncological outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1.3 Genetic pre-disposition
document_sections.content: Patients testing positive for Lynch syndrome are significantly younger and more frequently have ureteral UTUC. A prognostic effect has not been demonstrated to date.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1.4 Tobacco consumption
document_sections.content: Smoking at diagnosis increases disease-recurrence and mortality risks as well as intravesical recurrence after RNU. Smoking cessation over ten years improves outcomes to those observed in non-smokers.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1.5 Surgical delay
document_sections.content: Waiting between diagnosis and removal of an invasive tumour may raise progression risk. Once RNU is chosen, it should take place within twelve weeks; a delay below four weeks has been suggested for ureteral UTUC.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1.6 Other factors
document_sections.content: Greater comorbidity and worse scores on American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA), performance status (PS) and Charlson Comorbidity Index measures are associated with poorer survival across stages. Higher ASA score and poor PS predict worse CSS after RNU. Obesity and higher body mass index adversely affect cancer-specific outcomes after RNU, possibly with differences by race. Associations with locally advanced disease and cancer-specific mortality have been reported for high pre-treatment-derived neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio, low albumin, elevated C-reactive protein or modified Glasgow score, high De Ritis ratio, altered renal function and high fibrinogen.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2.1 Tumour stage and grade
document_sections.content: Stage and grade are the principal prognostic features; muscular invasion indicates poor prognosis. A large Dutch UTUC series reported 5-year CSS of 86% for non-muscleinvasive tumours, 70% for muscle-invasive organ-confined tumours and 44% for locally advanced tumours. A contemporary SEER RNU analysis in high-risk disease reported 5-year CSS of 86% for T1N0, 77% for T2N0, 63% for T3N0 and 39% for T4N0/T any N1–3. Subdivision of pT3 into pT3a and pT3b might be prognostically relevant, but high-quality validation is absent.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2.2.1 Multifocality
document_sections.content: Across studies, approximately 7-42% of UTUC patients have multifocal disease. Multifocality is associated with more advanced stage and poorer prognosis despite RNU, yet multifocal tumours can also arise in otherwise low-risk disease with a favourable prognosis. Studies differ in whether they define multifocality by lesion number or involvement of both renal pelvis and ureter. Multifocality alone cannot establish risk or determine whether kidney-sparing surgery is safe; classification as high-risk requires accompanying high-risk features.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2.2.2 Hydroureteronephrosis
document_sections.content: Hydroureteronephrosis is associated with advanced UTUC and poorer prognosis after RNU. A meta-analysis of 22 studies and 7,542 patients associated pre-operative hydroureteronephrosis significantly with ureteral location, advanced stage and nodal metastases. It independently predicted poorer overall, cancer-specific and disease-free survival, but not intravesical recurrence. Obstruction can nevertheless occur in low-risk disease, such as a pTa low-grade ureteral tumour. Hydroureteronephrosis alone cannot establish high risk or rule out safe kidney preservation; additional high-risk factors are needed.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2.2.3 Tumour size
document_sections.content: Larger ureteral and renal-pelvis tumours are more likely to be muscle-invasive or extend beyond the organ. A meta-analysis involving 32,292 patients associated greater size significantly with worse overall, cancer-specific and disease-free survival and with intravesical recurrence. For renal-pelvis UTUC, median tumour size is 3.5 to 4.0 cm, and each 1 cm increase corresponds to a 1.25-fold increase in risk of muscle-invasive disease at RNU. A multi-institutional study of 932 patients suggested 2 cm as the best threshold for identifying > pT2 UTUC. Size measurement lacks standardisation and varies between assessors. Size alone must not dictate treatment or high-risk assignment: a tumour exceeding 2 cm needs accompanying high-risk factors for that classification.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2.3 Pathological subtypes
document_sections.content: Histological subtypes are associated with poorer CSS and overall survival (OS). Micropapillary, squamous and sarcomatoid subtypes have been studied most and are consistently linked to locally advanced disease and worse outcomes. After shared decision-making, RNU should be proposed to patients with these subtypes because progression risk is higher.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2.4 Lymph node involvement
document_sections.content: Nodal metastases predict poor survival after surgery. Lymph-node density with a cut-off of 30% and extranodal extension strongly predict outcomes in N+ UTUC. Lymph node dissection (LND) during RNU improves staging accuracy, although whether it is curative remains disputed.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2.5 Lymphovascular invasion
document_sections.content: Lymphovascular invasion (LVI) occurs in approximately 20% of invasive UTUC and independently predicts survival. Every UTUC pathology report should explicitly state LVI status.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2.6 Surgical margins
document_sections.content: A positive soft-tissue margin increases recurrence risk after RNU. Pathology assessment should identify and report positive margins at ureteral transection, the bladder cuff and tissues surrounding the tumour.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2.7 Other pathological factors
document_sections.content: Necrosis affecting > 10% of tumour area independently predicts prognosis after RNU. Following neoadjuvant treatment, pathological downstaging is associated with better OS. Sessile architecture on RNU pathology predicts worse outcomes. Concomitant CIS in organ-confined UTUC and previous bladder CIS are associated with greater recurrence and cancer-specific mortality. Gross infiltration or invasion of peri-pelvic adipose tissue carries higher post-RNU recurrence risk than microscopic invasion of renal parenchyma.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.3 Molecular markers
document_sections.content: UTUC molecular studies are limited chiefly by retrospective design and, in most instances, small samples. No investigated molecular marker is validated for routine clinical decision-making.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 Risk stratification for clinical decision making
document_sections.content: Because clinical staging is difficult, distinguishing low from high progression risk helps identify candidates for kidney-sparing treatment versus RNU. Figure 6.1 shows the factors used for non-metastatic disease at risk of > pT2/non-organ-confined progression. Its low-risk category requires all of unifocal disease, tumour size < 2 cm, absence of high-grade cytology, low-grade URS biopsy and no invasive appearance on CT. Its strong high-risk criteria are high-grade cytology, high-grade URS biopsy, local invasion on CT or a histological subtype; any one meets that part of the definition. Multifocal disease, tumour size ≥ 2 cm and hydronephrosis are designated weak high-risk criteria. Individually treating size, multifocality or hydronephrosis as proxies for high risk has weak evidential support, especially in low-grade tumours; the kidney-sparing-versus-RNU choice in that setting warrants shared decision-making. Pre-RNU models predict > pT2 or non-organ-confined disease, and other models seek to refine kidney-sparing eligibility. Pre-operative and post-operative nomograms may inform counselling about surveillance and peri-operative chemotherapy, but substantial heterogeneity discourages systematic use despite moderate-to-good discrimination.

document_sections.heading: 6.3 Bladder recurrence
document_sections.content: A meta-analysis identified patient-, tumour- and treatment-specific predictors of bladder recurrence after RNU. Patient factors include male gender, previous BC, smoking and pre-operative chronic kidney disease. Tumour factors include positive pre-operative cytology, grade, ureteral location, multifocality, diameter, invasive pT stage and necrosis. Treatment factors include laparoscopic surgery, extravesical removal of the bladder cuff and positive surgical margins. Diagnostic URS has also been associated with higher post-RNU bladder recurrence risk. On evidence of only low quality, one intravesical chemotherapy dose after diagnostic or therapeutic ureteroscopy for non-metastatic UTUC has been suggested to reduce bladder recurrence, by analogy with treatment after RNU.

document_sections.heading: 6.4 Summary of evidence and recommendation for the prognosis of UTUC
document_sections.content: The evidence summary identifies size, stage, grade, multifocality, hydronephrosis and histological subtypes as important prognostic factors (LE 3); available models for pT2/non-organ-confined disease and post-RNU prognosis (LE 3); effects of patient, tumour and treatment features on bladder recurrence after kidney preservation or RNU (LE 3); and the absence of validated molecular biomarkers for clinical use (LE 3). Use of prognostic features to stratify risk and guide treatment is recommended (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 7. DISEASE MANAGEMENT
document_sections.content: Every patient whose imaging raises suspicion of UTUC should be discussed by a multidisciplinary team before treatment begins.

document_sections.heading: 7.1.1 General considerations on kidney-sparing surgery
document_sections.content: In low-risk UTUC, kidney-sparing surgery avoids some morbidity of RNU, including loss of renal function, without compromising oncological outcomes; survival is similar to that after RNU. It is the preferred approach and should be discussed in every low-risk case through shared decision-making, irrespective of contralateral kidney status.

document_sections.heading: 7.1.2 Ureteroscopy
document_sections.content: Endoscopic ablation should be considered for clinically low-risk tumours. Flexible ureteroscopy is useful for pelvicalyceal lesions. Complete tumour removal or destruction is necessary, and patients must understand and be able to comply with early second-look URS and stringent surveillance. Progression remains possible because imaging and biopsy imperfectly characterise risk and tumour biology. A systematic review found survival after endoscopy comparable with RNU, but more local recurrence and repeat procedures, with uncertainty about preservation of renal function over the long term.

document_sections.heading: 7.1.3 Percutaneous access
document_sections.content: Percutaneous treatment can be considered for low-risk renal-pelvis UTUC, including lower-calyceal lesions inaccessible or difficult to manage using flexible URS. Its use has declined as endoscopic instruments have improved. Tumour seeding remains a risk.

document_sections.heading: 7.1.4 Ureteral resection
document_sections.content: Segmental ureteral resection with adequate margins preserves the same-side kidney while supplying tissue for grading and staging. Resection involving the proximal two-thirds fails more often than distal resection. Distal ureterectomy with ureteroneocystostomy is indicated for low-risk distal-ureter tumours that cannot be fully removed endoscopically. Total ureterectomy with ileal-ureteral substitution, or renal autotransplantation with pyelocystostomy, is technically feasible only in selected low-risk cases in which preserving renal tissue is mandatory.

document_sections.heading: 7.1.5 Chemo-ablation
document_sections.content: A single-arm phase III study enrolled 71 patients with biopsy-confirmed low-grade UTUC measuring less than 15 mm. Retrograde renal-pelvis and calyceal instillation of mitomycin-containing reverse thermal gel (UGN-101) for 6 weekly induction treatments produced complete response in 41 patients (58%). Frequently reported adverse events of any cause were ureteric stenosis in 31 (44%), urinary tract infection in 23 (32%), haematuria in 22 (31%), flank pain in 21 (30%) and nausea in 17 (24%); treatment was required for stenosis in 19/31 (61%). Of the 41 complete responders, 29 received at least one maintenance instillation, with a median of 6; 23/41 (56%) remained disease free at one year.

document_sections.heading: 7.1.6.1 Upper urinary tract
document_sections.content: Following complete tumour eradication with kidney preservation, antegrade BCG or mitomycin C instillation through a percutaneous nephrostomy has been investigated for upper-tract CIS; retrograde administration through an open-ended single-J ureteric stent is also used. Either route requires a preceding nephro-ureterogram to exclude obstruction or leakage, assessment to exclude infection and a low-pressure system to prevent pyelovenous influx. Delivery via reflux around a double-J stent is suboptimal because treatment often fails to reach the renal pelvis. A systematic review and meta-analysis of adjuvant endocavitary chemotherapy and/or BCG for papillary non-invasive Ta–T1 UTUC and BCG for upper-tract CIS found no administration-route difference in recurrence, progression, CSS or OS. Included studies were underpowered, highly heterogeneous, small and retrospective, with publication and reporting biases. Recurrence after instillation was comparable to published rates without treatment, leaving efficacy in question. More recent evidence suggests one early upper-tract instillation of mitomycin C might reduce local recurrence in low-grade UTUC; the investigators reported limited complications and proposed retrograde pyelography first to exclude contrast leakage. Randomised evaluation remains necessary.

document_sections.heading: 7.1.6.2 Bladder
document_sections.content: Existing randomised trials included RNU recipients only; no current data support intravesical chemotherapy after kidney-sparing surgery.

document_sections.heading: 7.1.7 Recommendation for kidney-sparing management of localised low-risk UTUC
document_sections.content: Kidney-sparing management is recommended as the primary treatment choice for low-risk tumours (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 7.2.1.1.1 Open radical nephroureterectomy
document_sections.content: Open RNU with bladder-cuff excision is standard for high-risk UTUC regardless of location. Oncological surgical principles must be followed to prevent tumour seeding.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.1.1.2 Minimal invasive radical nephroureterectomy
document_sections.content: Manipulating large tumours under pneumoperitoneum can lead to retroperitoneal or trocar-tract metastatic spread. Precautions include avoiding entry into the urinary tract except for bladder-cuff excision after clipping the ureter and draining the bladder, preventing instrument contact with tumour, operating in a closed system without morcellation, using an extraction bag and removing kidney, ureter and bladder cuff together. An open approach is favoured for invasive or large T3/T4 and/or N+/M+ tumours because oncological outcomes may be better. Laparoscopic RNU is safe with experienced operators applying strict oncological principles, and several studies suggest outcomes resembling open RNU. A small randomised study of n = 80 instead found laparoscopy inferior in non-organ-confined disease. Despite advances in staging and surgery, post-RNU oncological outcomes have not significantly changed over the past three decades. A population dataset associated centres treating > 6 RNU patients yearly with improved 30- and 90-day mortality and long-term overall survival. Robot-assisted laparoscopy can be considered: peri-operative benefits resemble standard laparoscopy, and data suggest oncological equivalence across approaches. Both laparoscopic and robotic RNU may, however, carry higher intravesical recurrence risk than open surgery.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.1.1.3 Bladder cuff management
document_sections.content: The distal ureter and ureteral orifice are removed because recurrence there and in the bladder is a substantial risk. The pluck technique, stripping, transurethral intramural-ureter resection and intussusception have been used to simplify removal, but none has convincingly demonstrated equivalence to complete bladder-cuff excision.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.1.1.4 Lymph node dissection
document_sections.content: The anatomical LND template probably matters more for survival than the number of removed nodes. Complete template-based LND improves CSS in muscle-invasive disease and reduces local recurrence; survival benefits have also been reported among clinically and pathologically node-negative patients. Nodal-metastasis risk rises with stage. Although LND appears unnecessary for TaT1 tumours because nodal spread is uncommon, pre-operative stage assessment is unreliable; template-based LND should therefore be offered when RNU is planned for high-risk UTUC.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.2 Distal ureterectomy
document_sections.content: For high-risk UTUC confined to the distal ureter, distal ureterectomy appears to have outcomes similar to RNU and may be combined with LND. Because supporting evidence is weak, it should currently be restricted to highly selected patients whose likely benefits outweigh potential risks.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.3 Kidney-sparing surgery for imperative indications
document_sections.content: URS or segmental ureterectomy may be considered individually for high-risk patients with imperative reasons to preserve a kidney, including a solitary kidney, bilateral UTUC, severe chronic kidney disease or comorbidity that compromises RNU. Compared with low-risk UTUC, high-risk disease has greater progression risk after kidney preservation, directly affecting survival.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.4.1.1 Chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) permits cisplatin-based treatment before RNU-related loss of renal function. Retrospective studies report pathological downstaging and complete responses at RNU, an association with OS, and lower recurrence and mortality than RNU alone without compromising definitive surgery; an OS benefit is possible. No RCT has yet been published. Prospective phase II studies of cisplatin-combination NAC in high-grade and/or cT2-T4N0M0 UTUC reported 14 - 19% pathological complete responses and a final stage < ypT1 in more than 60%, with an acceptable toxicity profile. A systematic review and meta-analysis of more than 800 patients found 43% pathological partial response and 33% downstaging, alongside OS and CSS benefit versus RNU alone. These pooled findings are not conclusive because of substantial bias and heterogeneity and failure to separate genuinely neoadjuvant from downstaging chemotherapy.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.4.1.2 Immunotherapy
document_sections.content: The only described neoadjuvant pembrolizumab assessment was a small phase II study of 10 high-risk UTUC patients: it observed no pathological responses and reported one treatment-related death. Current evidence does not support neoadjuvant immunotherapy for high-risk UTUC.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.4.2.1 Bladder instillations
document_sections.content: Post-RNU bladder recurrence occurs in 22–47%. Two prospective randomised trials and two meta-analyses found that one intravesical chemotherapy dose, using mitomycin C or pirarubicin, at 2–10 days after RNU lowers bladder-tumour recurrence in the first postoperative years among patients without previous BC. A cystogram may be considered beforehand if extravasation is a concern. All studies reported very low adverse-event risk. Administration during RNU before opening the bladder cuff has also been reported safe and avoids a later cystogram, but efficacy evidence is limited. More than one peri-operative instillation is unlikely to materially improve prevention. Direct supporting evidence after kidney-sparing surgery is absent, though a single dose might also work there. One study with low-level evidence suggested bladder irrigation might reduce recurrence after RNU.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.4.2.2 Systemic Chemotherapy
document_sections.content: A multicentre phase III prospective RCT of n = 261 compared surveillance with four cycles of adjuvant gemcitabineplatinum chemotherapy begun within 90 days after RNU in pT2–pT4, N (any) or positive (pT any, N1–3) M0 UTUC. It reported significantly improved disease-free survival: 3 year DFS 71% vs 50%; 5 year DFS 63% vs 46%; HR 0.54 ; CI 0.36-0.79. For 3 & 5 year MFS, the reported improvement was 19 %, HR 0.55 CI 0.0.36-0.77; the latter interval is written that way in the document. Assignment to gemcitabine/cisplatin or gemcitabine/carboplatin used GFR alone, and benefit appeared with either type. OS showed a non-significant favourable trend of 12% at 3 years; early closure after the primary 3 year DFS endpoint left the trial underpowered for OS. Renal deterioration after RNU may prevent cisplatin administration; a review reported GFR of around 50 mls/min at three months. Split-dose cisplatin with hydration may be considered at GFR down to 45 mL/min. Table 2 specifies platinum eligibility and states that Carboplatin is not indicated for neoadjuvant treatment. In a retrospective study, adjuvant chemotherapy was associated with OS benefit only for pure UC among histological subtypes; nevertheless, it should be considered if UC predominates in the pathology.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.4.2.3 Immunotherapy
document_sections.content: In a multicentre, double-blind phase III RCT after radical surgery for high-risk muscle-invasive UC, including pT3, pT4a or pN+ disease, nivolumab improved disease-free survival versus placebo in the intention-to-treat group (20.8 vs. 10.8 months) and in patients with programmed death-ligand 1 (PDL1) expression of 1% or more. Most participants had BC after cystectomy; a smaller group had UTUC after RNU. Median recurrence-free survival outside the urinary tract was 22.9 months with nivolumab and 13.7 months with placebo in the entire intention-to-treat group. Treatment-related events > grade 3 occurred in 17.9% and 7.2%, respectively. The UTUC subgroup did not appear to benefit; more follow-up and analysis are needed. Nonetheless, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) approved adjuvant nivolumab monotherapy for high-recurrence-risk muscle-invasive UC after radical surgery with tumour-cell PD-L1 expression > 1% when adjuvant chemotherapy is declined or unsuitable. A network meta-analysis suggests greater oncological benefit from adjuvant platinum chemotherapy than immune checkpoint inhibitors after radical surgery for UTUC.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.4.2.4 Radiotherapy
document_sections.content: Adjuvant radiation has been proposed for loco-regional control after surgery, but available data are conflicting and insufficient for conclusions. Its additional value alongside chemotherapy remains uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the management of high-risk non-metastatic UTUC
document_sections.content: The evidence summary describes RNU as standard for high-risk disease irrespective of location (LE 2a), similar outcomes for open, laparoscopic and robotic surgery in organ-confined disease (LE 2a), increased BC recurrence if the bladder cuff is incompletely removed (LE 3), improved survival with lymphadenectomy in muscle-invasive UTUC (LE 3), improved disease-free survival after postoperative platinum chemotherapy (LE 1b), and fewer BC recurrences after one postoperative intravesical chemotherapy instillation (LE 1b). Recommendations are RNU for high-risk non-metastatic UTUC (Strong); open RNU for non-organ-confined disease (Weak); template-based lymphadenectomy (Weak); adjuvant platinum chemotherapy after RNU for eligible pT2–T4 and/or pN+ patients (Strong); postoperative bladder chemotherapy for patients without prior BC (Strong); discussion of adjuvant nivolumab if platinum is unsuitable or declined for > pT3 and/or pN+ after RNU alone or > ypT2 and/or ypN+ after NAC followed by RNU (Weak); distal ureterectomy for selected high-risk distal-ureter tumours (Weak); and individual shared discussion of kidney preservation when there is an imperative indication, acknowledging greater progression risk (Strong). Figures 7.1 and 7.2 depict diagnostic assessment, risk-based treatment and surgical choices by tumour location. Their cautions favour considering a more conservative approach with a solitary kidney or low-grade disease lacking invasive features.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.1 Clinical loco-regional lymph node metastases
document_sections.content: The best treatment for clinically node-positive UTUC is not established. Clinically N+ patients should be offered first-line platinum-based chemotherapy for downstaging. Maintenance avelumab can be offered after response or stable disease, particularly in cN2. In those responding to initial systemic therapy, the team and patient can discuss resection with LND according to nodal extent, such as cN1/N2. Progression may prompt second-line treatment resembling that for metastatic disease.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.1.1 Enfortumab vedotin + pembrolizumab combination therapy
document_sections.content: Platinum chemotherapy had remained standard for previously untreated advanced or metastatic UC for more than 23 years. In October 2023, the phase III multicentre randomised EV302 study compared enfortumab vedotin, a nectin 4-directed antibody–drug conjugate, plus the checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab (EV+P), against platinum combinations with gemcitabine-cisplatin or gemcitabine -carboplatin. It reported significantly improved PFS ( HR 0.45 (0.38-0.54 ) and OS (HR 0.47 (0.38-0.58), a response rate of 68% versus 44%, and complete response of 29%. OS benefit occurred across subgroups regardless of cisplatin eligibility. Common grade 3 or higher treatment-related events of special interest were skin reactions (15.5%), peripheral neuropathy (6.8%) and hyperglycaemia (6.1%). The UTUC proportion in that study was not yet known. The best treatment sequence after Ev+Pembro remains uncertain and depends on drugs previously received.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.1.2 Patients ineligible for EV+Pembro and fit for cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Upper-tract and bladder UC both respond to systemic platinum chemotherapy; metastatic-setting eligibility uses the criteria in Table 2. A retrospective analysis of three RCTs found no PFS or OS effect of upper versus lower primary-tumour location among patients given platinum combinations for locally advanced or metastatic UC. Consequently, cisplatin-containing combinations are standard for advanced or metastatic UTUC when EV + Pembro is unsuitable. Several cisplatin combinations have demonstrated efficacy; gemcitabine with cisplatin is used most widely. Cisplatin is widely considered at eGFR > 45 mL/min. Earlier first-line trials of PD1 or PD-L1 inhibitors, alone or combined with platinum chemotherapy, did not show a significant survival advantage and therefore those approaches were not previously recommended; these studies included cisplatin and carboplatin combinations. A subsequent phase III RCT found that adding nivolumab to gemcitabine-cisplatin improved median OS from 18.9 months to 21.7 months, HR 0.78 (0.63-0.96), and median PFS from 7.6 months to 7.9 months, HR 0.72 (0.59-0.88). Objective response rates were 43.1 % with chemotherapy alone versus 57.6% with the addition. UTUC accounted for 12.6%, but location-specific subgroup results were unavailable.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.1.3 Patients ineligible for Ev+Pembro and unfit for cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Carboplatin-based chemotherapy is recommended if cisplatin is unsuitable, with carboplatin plus gemcitabine preferred regardless of PDL-1 status. A critical re-analysis of advanced-UC RCTs comparing cisplatin and carboplatin combinations found a small OS advantage for cisplatin.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.1.4 Maintenance therapy after first-line platinum-based chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Maintenance avelumab is recommended only after first-line platinum chemotherapy, for complete response, partial response or stable disease following 4–6 cycles. A phase III RCT started maintenance within 10 weeks of completing 4 to 6 cycles of gemcitabine plus cisplatin or carboplatin; among advanced or metastatic UC patients without progression, OS was significantly longer than with best supportive care alone (HR: 0.69; 95% CI: 0.56–0.86), and median OS increased from 14 to 21 months. Almost 30% had UTUC, but outcomes were not analysed by tumour location. In a separate phase II study of 108 metastatic-UC patients with at least stable disease after first-line platinum therapy, maintenance pembrolizumab improved PFS over placebo (5.4 vs. 3.0 months).

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.1.5 Patients unfit for any combination therapy
document_sections.content: Pembrolizumab or atezolizumab are alternative options when a patient is PD-L1 positive and cannot receive platinum-based chemotherapy. In a single-arm phase II cisplatin-ineligible UC trial (n = 370), pembrolizumab monotherapy produced a 26% objective response rate in 69 metastatic UTUC patients; across the whole cohort, PD-L1 expression of 10% was associated with greater response. Toxicity resembled previous studies. In another single-arm phase II cisplatin-ineligible UC trial (n = 119), atezolizumab monotherapy produced a 39% objective response rate in 33 (28%) metastatic UTUC patients. Median OS of the overall study cohort was 15.9 months, and treatment-related toxicity resembled previous reports.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.2 Systemic treatments - later line setting
document_sections.content: Selection of later systemic therapy depends on which agents were used first.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.2.1 Platinum based chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Platinum-based chemotherapy should be the preferred second-line treatment if it was not administered first-line. Evidence does not support maintenance avelumab outside the first-line setting.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.2.2 Immunotherapy
document_sections.content: In a phase III RCT of 542 patients previously treated with platinum for advanced UC, pembrolizumab lowered mortality risk versus investigator-selected paclitaxel, docetaxel or vinflunine: median OS was 10.3 months versus 7.4 months, HR: 0.73; 95% CI: 0.59–0.91. Responses were more frequent and durable with pembrolizumab (21% vs. 11%); in its UTUC subgroup (n = 75/13.8%), the OS benefit appeared larger (50%). The IMVigor211 study of PD-L1-positive disease relapsing after platinum found no significant OS improvement for atezolizumab compared with second-line chemotherapy. Single-arm phase I or II studies of nivolumab, avelumab and durvalumab in platinum-resistant metastatic UC reported objective response rates from 17.8% to 19.6% and median OS from 7.7 months to 18.2 months. UTUC representation was specified only for avelumab (n = 7/15.9%), without site-specific outcome analysis. A multicentre phase I/II study of nivolumab plus ipilimumab in 78 patients progressing after platinum reported significant antitumour activity and objective response up to 38%, but no UTUC subgroup analysis. Evidence for other second-line immunotherapy combinations remains limited.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.2.3 Novel agents
document_sections.content: Erdafitinib is described as a pan-FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting FGFR1–4. In a phase II study of 99 patients with locally advanced or metastatic UC progressing after first-line chemotherapy and FGFR DNA genomic alterations, defined there as FGFR2/3 fusions or FGFR3 mutations, its RECIST radiological response rate was 40%. Among 23 participants with UTUC and visceral metastases, radiological response was 43%. The phase III Thor study randomised 266 previously treated patients with similar alterations after 1-2 treatment lines to erdafitinib or investigator-chosen vinfunine or docetaxel. It reported significantly improved median OS by 4.3 months (HR 0.64;CI 0.47-0.88), PFS by 2.9 months (58; CI 0.44-0.78), and a 36% reduction in death risk; 33.5 % had UTUC. Because activating FGFR3 alterations are more frequent in UTUC than BC, a greater effect from targeting FGFR3 is anticipated, not established. UTUC patients should be tested for FGFR alterations, described for pre-treatment testing as FGFR2/3 mutations or FGFR3 fusions, before erdafitinib. In a phase II trial of 89 cisplatin-unfit metastatic-UC patients progressing after PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibition, 43% had UTUC; enfortumab vedotin yielded a 52% RECIST radiological response rate, including complete response in 20%. A phase III trial after platinum chemotherapy and progression during or after PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibition found longer median OS with enfortumab vedotin than standard chemotherapy (12.88 vs. 8.97 months). An open-label phase II trial gave sacituzumab govitecan to 108 metastatic-UC patients progressing after platinum and checkpoint inhibitors; radiological response was 27%, median response duration 7.2 months, median PFS 5.4 months and median OS 10.9 months. The publication did not specify the UTUC fraction. A prespecified RANGE subgroup analysis after progression on both platinum and checkpoint therapy reported median PFS of 3.15 months with ramucirumab/docetaxel versus 2.73 months with placebo/docetaxel (HR: 0.786; 95% CI: 0.404–1.528, p = 0.4877). Although the ramucirumab arm contained more patients with poor prognostic features, its apparent favourable trend needs confirmation because patient numbers were limited and treatment arms imbalanced.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.3.1 Radical nephroureterectomy
document_sections.content: Evidence for RNU in metastatic UTUC is sparse and mainly retrospective and observational. Selected patients, particularly those able to receive cisplatin, may obtain CSS or OS benefit, potentially limited to individuals with only one metastatic site. Given substantial bias risk, metastatic-setting RNU should chiefly be reserved for palliation and control of symptomatic disease.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.3.2 Metastasectomy
document_sections.content: No study specific to UTUC establishes benefit from metastasectomy in advanced disease. Reports suggesting safety or oncological benefit in selected individuals require caution. Without RCT evidence, suitability must be evaluated individually and any decision for surgical metastasectomy made jointly with the patient.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the treatment of metastatic UTUC
document_sections.content: The evidence summary reports first-line OS benefit for Enfortmab vedotin + Pembrolizumab over gemcitabinecisplatin (LE 1b); improved median survival with cisplatin combinations (LE 2); cisplatin combinations as standard when cisplatin is tolerated but Enfortumab + Pembrolizumab is unsuitable (LE 1b); additional first-line survival benefit from nivolumab with cisplatin chemotherapy (LE 1b); and benefit from carboplatin combinations if cisplatin is unsuitable (LE 1b). Non-platinum combinations have not been compared against standard chemotherapy in either cisplatin-fit or cisplatin-unfit groups (LE 4). Maintenance avelumab improves OS versus supportive care after no progression on 4 to 6 cycles of gemcitabine plus cisplatin or carboplatin (LE 1b). The summary records approvals of post-platinum pembrolizumab (LE 1b) and nivolumab (LE 2a) when prior immunotherapy was not given, and first-line pembrolizumab or atezolizumab restricted to PD-L1-positive patients unsuitable for platinum (each LE 2a). It associates erdafitinib with improved OS in platinum-refractory FGFR-altered UC (LE 1b), and enfortumab vedotin with OS benefit after platinum and subsequent progression during or after PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibition (LE 1b). Palliative nephroureterectomy may improve quality of life through symptom control (LE 3); selected metastatic patients may gain survival from RNU, for example after platinum response with limited metastatic burden (LE 4). The recommendations are first-line Enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab in advanced/metastatic disease (Strong); if that combination is unsuitable, a platinum combination for platinum-eligible patients (Strong), gemcitabine-cisplatin + nivolumab for cisplatin-eligible patients (Weak), gemcitabine/cisplatin or HD-MVAC for cisplatin-eligible patients (Strong), and gemcitabine/carboplatin if cisplatin-ineligible (Strong). Offer maintenance avelumab after no progression on 4 to 6 first-line platinum-combination cycles (Strong). For PD-L1-positive patients unable to receive any combination, offer pembrolizumab or atezolizumab (Weak). In later lines, offer a platinum combination second-line if not given first-line (Strong); offer pembrolizumab after progression during or after platinum combinations if maintenance avelumab was not received (Strong); and offer enfortumab vedotin after platinum and progression during or after a PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitor (Strong). Test for FGFR alterations, specified as FGFR2/3 mutations or FGFR3 fusions, before erdafitinib (Strong); offer erdafitinib as a subsequent-line alternative if platinum was previously given, disease progressed during or after PD-1 or PD-L1 treatment, and the specified FGFR alteration is present (Strong). Offer vinflunine second-line only if immunotherapy or combination chemotherapy is infeasible, or use it third-line or later (Strong). Offer nephroureterectomy for palliation of symptomatic, resectable locally advanced tumours (Weak). Figure 7.3 sets out eligibility-based first-line and later-line options; its gemcitabine-cisplatin plus nivolumab branch carries a caution about unavailable UTUC subgroup-analysis data.

document_sections.heading: 8. FOLLOW-UP
document_sections.content: Surveillance after UTUC treatment aims to address rehabilitation needs and detect urothelial recurrence or a new primary tumour and regional or distant spread; bladder recurrence is not classified as distant recurrence. Marked heterogeneity among recurrence studies means follow-up recommendations have, at best, low-level evidence. After RNU for low-risk disease, follow the low-risk NMIBC bladder protocol: cystoscopy at three months, again 9 months later, then yearly for 5 years. Metastasis screening is not obligatory; routine contralateral-upper-tract imaging should be decided individually because recurrence there is uncommon. High-risk RNU requires stringent surveillance for metachronous bladder cancer, local recurrence and distant spread; bladder-tumour probability rises with time, although bladder and other-site recurrence risks fall 4 years after RNU, potentially allowing less intensive annual cystoscopy and cross-sectional imaging, including CT urography, thereafter. Following kidney preservation for low-risk UTUC, if early second-look URS at 6-8 weeks or a segmental-resection specimen shows no upgrading or upstaging, perform cystoscopy and CT urography at 3 and 6 months and then yearly for 5 years. Bladder recurrence beyond 5 years is limited to 6%. After kidney preservation for high-risk disease, whether treatment was imperative affects surveillance because consequences of recurrence differ; the ipsilateral upper tract needs careful long-term monitoring because recurrence and progression remain possible even beyond 5 years. Surveillance generally uses CT urography, cystoscopy and cytology. Unresolved issues include the value of new urinary markers versus voided cytology; effects of the Paris System on voided and selective cytology accuracy, especially for high-risk disease; whether adjuvant upper-tract instillation permits less intensive follow-up; and the role of ipsilateral URS compared with CT urography and voided cytology after endourological preservation. Optimal screening and long-term surveillance for Lynch syndrome, with or without previous UTUC, are unknown, particularly for MSH2 carriers; surveillance based on testing for nonvisible haematuria or urine cytology is inadequate.

document_sections.heading: 8.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the follow-up of UTUC
document_sections.content: The evidence summary states that follow-up should depend on risk and treatment type (LE 3). Following RNU for low-risk disease, perform cystoscopy at three months; if negative, repeat 9 months later and yearly for 5 years (Weak). Following RNU for high-risk disease, perform cystoscopy and cytology at 3 months; if negative, repeat both every 3 months for 2 years, every 6 months until 5 years, then yearly (Weak). Also perform CT urography and chest CT every 6 months for 2 years, then yearly (Weak). After kidney-sparing treatment for low-risk disease, obtain cystoscopy and CT urography at 3 and 6 months and yearly for 5 years (Weak); perform URS at 3 months if no second-look URS occurred (Weak). After kidney-sparing treatment for high-risk disease, perform second-look URS and cytology in 6 weeks and, if no tumour remains, use follow-up principles resembling those after RNU for high-risk disease (Weak).
